note: Summaries are written by Claude from each paper's abstract. Items marked 'title only' had no abstract available — open the paper before relying on them.

items.title: A QSVT-Based Quantum Jacobi Algorithm for Linear Systems with Application to the Poisson Equation
items.authors: L. M. Piskol, T. Grahs, S. Langer

summary.problem: Most quantum linear solvers try to invert the matrix directly, while CFD codes rely on iterative methods such as Jacobi.
summary.method: The Jacobi iteration is written as a polynomial of a block-encoded operator using quantum singular value transformation (QSVT), and tested on 1D and 2D Poisson problems — including the pressure Poisson equation inside Chorin's projection method for lid-driven cavity flow.
summary.result: The number of ancilla qubits stays constant as iterations increase; circuit depth grows linearly with the number of Jacobi iterations.

items.why: The closest paper to your quantum pressure-solver study: it uses exactly Chorin's projection step. Compare its iteration-count argument with your condition-number numbers — Jacobi needs O(κ) iterations, so your multiphase κ would make the circuit very deep.

items.title: Quantum Algorithms for Computational Fluid Dynamics
items.authors: M. G. Cecile, N.-L. van Hülst, T. Hashizume et al.

summary.problem: Which quantum approaches could realistically solve the PDEs behind CFD?
summary.method: Reviews quantum linear solvers (HHL to QSVT), Hamiltonian simulation, quantum lattice Boltzmann and tensor networks, and tests them on benchmark PDEs such as Poisson and reaction–diffusion.
summary.result: Any advantage is strongly problem-dependent, governed above all by the condition number and the cost of state preparation.

items.why: A current review to cite in the quantum section of your Poisson note, and a good map of methods beyond HHL/VQLS.

items.title: Bubble detachment from solid surfaces induced by impacting particles
items.authors: X. Chen, X. Li, B. Yin et al.

summary.problem: How does a particle striking a wall-attached bubble make it detach?
summary.method: A coupled VOF/level-set method combined with an immersed boundary method and discrete element method, extended to an axisymmetric configuration.
summary.result: Three detachment modes are identified: capillary-wave, bubble-rebound and particle-rebound.

items.why: Combines the three ingredients of your thesis — VOF interface, immersed solid, and a wall-attached interface — in a JFM paper. Check how they treat the contact angle on the wall while the particle moves.

items.title: A three-dimensional numerical scheme for modeling contact line pinning on heterogeneous substrates
items.authors: S. K. Nayak, A. Bhattacharya, P. M. Nair

summary.method: From the title: a 3D numerical scheme for contact-line pinning on chemically or physically heterogeneous walls.
summary.result: Open the paper to see results.

items.why: Pinning and hysteresis are the natural next step beyond a single equilibrium contact angle in your three-phase work. Worth reading the method section.

items.title: A conservative cut-cell/front-tracking method for interface-resolved two-phase flow simulations
items.authors: D. Dupuy, A. Toutant, A. du Cluzeau

summary.problem: One-field models smear the interface, and front tracking needs a conservative way to represent the interface on a fixed grid.
summary.method: Lagrangian front-tracking markers combined with a cut-cell finite-volume discretisation on a staggered Cartesian grid, a projection method, and volume-preserving mesh motion for mass conservation.
summary.result: Stable and more accurate than a one-field/front-tracking baseline on static and oscillating droplets, bubble arrays, a rising bubble and zig-zagging bubbles.

items.why: A strong competitor to VOF/PLIC on mass conservation. Useful for the 'why VOF?' question at your defense — know its pros and cons.

items.title: A multicolor coupled level set and volume-of-fluid framework for controlled coalescence of drops and bubbles in two-phase flow simulations
items.authors: S. Basak, U. C. Bitencourt, G. B. Deane et al.

summary.method: From the title: several colour functions (one per drop or bubble) with coupled level set and VOF, so that numerical coalescence can be controlled.
summary.result: Open the paper to see results.

items.why: Multiple colour functions are close to how you handle three phases. See how they reconstruct interfaces when two colours share a cell.

items.title: Towards Rapid Prototyping of Spray Injectors: A Regime-Agnostic Neural Operator Surrogate for Gas-Liquid Interface Evolution
items.authors: P. Guida, P.-H. Chen, H. G. Im et al.

summary.problem: Spray interfaces are hard to measure and expensive to simulate at fine scales.
summary.method: A boundary-conditioned Fourier Neural Operator predicts the evolution of a signed-distance function, trained on 2D VOF simulations, with optional physics-based regularizers.
summary.result: The signed-distance FNO keeps the interface sharper than a volume-fraction FNO but is still behind a U-Net; adding physics terms barely changed forecast error.

items.why: An honest negative-ish result on physics regularization — compare with your Young's-equation loss for PLIC-Net. Also note: predicting α directly loses sharpness, which supports your choice to learn local geometry instead.

items.title: Immersed boundary method of ghost cells for modelling flows in complex geometries with thermal effects and fluid–structure interaction
items.authors: J. E. F. Martini, A. da Silveira Neto

summary.problem: Simulating flow, heat transfer and FSI in complex geometries with a sharp-interface method.
summary.method: A 3D ghost-cell immersed boundary method in a parallel adaptive-mesh-refinement solver, with LES for high Reynolds numbers.
summary.result: Verified on several benchmarks, including a sphere at Re = 1000 and 5000; FSI natural frequencies for five vibration modes match the reference.

items.why: A sharp-interface (ghost-cell) alternative to your group's fictitious-domain approach. Good for the literature section of your FSI chapter.

items.title: An unconditionally stable explicit Robin–Robin partitioned scheme for fluid–structure interaction
items.authors: S. Guo, P. Lin, Y. Wang

summary.method: From the title: an explicit partitioned FSI coupling with Robin interface conditions, claimed unconditionally stable.
summary.result: Open the paper to see results.

items.why: Relevant to your earlier FSI-coupling study: explicit partitioned schemes usually suffer from the added-mass instability. Robin–Robin coupling is one of the standard cures.

items.title: Self-similar effective-to-apparent contact line length ratio in droplet friction on textured surfaces
items.authors: Y. Jiang, C. Wei, B. Li et al.

summary.problem: Droplet friction on textured superhydrophobic surfaces is hard to predict because the contact-line length that actually pins is poorly defined.
summary.method: Defines an effective-to-apparent contact-line length ratio and tests it with adhesion-force, contact-line and shape measurements on micropillar surfaces.
summary.result: The model predicts droplet friction across microstructure size, intrinsic wettability and droplet volume.

items.why: Experimental data on contact-line pinning — a possible validation target if you extend your model to textured walls.

items.title: Theory of the coalescence of two spherical liquid drops at early times
items.authors: R. Brandão, J. Eggers, M. A. Fontelos

summary.problem: The early-time dynamics of two equal drops merging under surface tension lack a full theory.
summary.method: Matched asymptotic expansions for the growth of the liquid bridge and the shape of the gap.
summary.result: Gives the bridge growth and gap shape as functions of the Ohnesorge number Oh = η/√(ργR).

items.why: A clean analytical benchmark for any VOF code's coalescence behaviour — and an example of the inner/outer matching from today's classics.

items.title: Physics-informed neural networks for planar interface evaporation: forward, inverse, and parameterized modeling
items.authors: T.-H. Phan, L. M. Pirnstill, F. Naderi et al.
items.venue: Int. J. Heat and Mass Transfer

summary.problem: Modelling a moving liquid–vapour evaporation interface with sharp gradients.
summary.method: PINNs solve a 1D unsteady Stefan problem coupled to a VOF transport equation, in forward, inverse and parameterized settings.
summary.result: The inverse setting recovers wall superheat, vapour conductivity and latent heat with errors below 7%, even with noisy data.

items.why: PINNs + VOF in 1D. Useful context for the 'ML for interfaces' landscape in your proposal.

items.title: Color-gradient lattice Boltzmann modeling of wetting boundary condition on curved solid boundaries
items.authors: M. Bhattacharya, S. Dash, S. Agarwal et al.

summary.method: From the title: a wetting (contact-angle) boundary condition for curved solid walls in colour-gradient LBM.
summary.result: Open the paper to see results.

items.why: Imposing a contact angle on a curved solid is exactly your hemisphere and sphere test cases. Compare their approach with your PLIC-based treatment.

items.title: Towards high-density-ratio multiphase flow: surface tension adjustment in the three-dimensional cumulant lattice Boltzmann method

summary.problem: Lattice Boltzmann multiphase methods struggle at high density ratios and produce spurious currents.
summary.method: A surface-tension adjustment for the 3D cumulant LBM.
summary.result: Reduced spurious currents and stable simulations at higher density ratios.

items.why: Shows how other communities attack the same density-ratio and parasitic-current problems that you face in the pressure solve.
